title: The Wow! signal
hook: In 1977, a telescope in Ohio heard something from deep space. Once.

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: The Big Ear radio telescope was scanning the sky for alien signals.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: For seventy-two seconds, a signal came in about thirty times stronger than the background noise.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the code on the printout and wrote one word: Wow!

beats.label: CLUE 3
beats.line: It came from Sagittarius, on the hydrogen frequency, a channel aliens might choose.

beats.label: THEORY
beats.line: A comet? Tested and rejected. A satellite? None were up there.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: Astronomers have listened for it many times since. It has never come back.

end.line: Was someone out there calling us?

description: On August 15, 1977 the Big Ear telescope recorded a 72-second signal from the direction of Sagittarius. It was never detected again.

facts.claim: The Wow! signal was recorded on 15 August 1977 by Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope (Delaware, Ohio).
facts.source: Wikipedia: Wow! signal; Ohio State University

facts.claim: The signal lasted the full 72-second observation window of the telescope.
Its peak intensity was about 30 times the background noise (the 'U' in 6EQUJ5, about 30 sigma).
Jerry Ehman circled the sequence 6EQUJ5 on the printout and wrote 'Wow!'.
The signal came from the direction of Sagittarius at about 1420.4556 MHz, close to the hydrogen line (1420.406 MHz).
A 2017 comet hypothesis was widely rejected by astronomers; no known satellites or aircraft matched.
Despite many follow-up searches, the signal was never detected again.
